items.en: The Sphere of Boundless Space: Its Realization

zh: 第二、明證虛空定，亦為六意：一、證相；二、明有支無支；三、體用；四、淺深；五、進退；六、功德。第一、明證相者，行者既一心念空不捨，則其心泯然，任運自住空緣。此亦似如前說未到地之相。於後豁然，與空相應，其心明淨，不苦不樂，益更增長，於深定中唯見虛空，無諸色相。雖緣無邊虛空，心無分散。既無色縛，心識澄靜，無礙自在，如鳥在籠中，籠破得出，飛騰自在。證虛空定亦復如是。復次，得空處定，出過色界，故名過一切色相。空法持心，種種諸色而不得起，故名滅有對相。既得勝妙空處，決定能捨色法，心不憶戀，故名不念種種相。是故經中多以此義明證虛空處定。
en: Second, clarifying the realization of the concentration of empty space: this too has six parts — the mark of realization; clarifying whether factors are present or absent; substance and function; depth; progress and regression; and merit.

First, clarifying the mark of realization: the practitioner, holding the mind single-mindedly on emptiness without relinquishing it, the mind grows indistinct, abiding of its own accord, spontaneously, within emptiness as its object. This, too, resembles the mark of the "not-yet-arrived" state already described above. Afterward, the mind opens out, corresponding with emptiness, bright and pure, free of both suffering and happiness, this state growing ever further — within this deep concentration, one sees only empty space itself, with no mark of form present at all. Although taking boundless empty space as its object, the mind is free of any scattering. Freed now from the bondage of form, mind and consciousness are clear and still, unobstructed and at ease — like a bird within a cage, the cage broken open, able to fly forth freely. The realization of the concentration of empty space is exactly the same.

Furthermore: having attained the concentration of the sphere of space, one has passed entirely beyond the form realm — hence this is named "passing beyond every mark of form." The dharma of emptiness sustains the mind, and the various forms are no longer able to arise at all — hence this is named "extinguishing the mark of resistance." Having attained this excellent, wondrous sphere of space, one is decisively able to relinquish the dharma of form, the mind no longer dwelling on or longing for it — hence this is named "no longer taking up any of the various marks." Hence the sūtras, for the most part, use this very sense to clarify the realization of the concentration of the sphere of space.

zh: 第二、明有支無支者，餘經論中明四無色定，例不立支，唯《纓絡經》云：「四空定，五支為因，第六默然心為定體，方便道同，體用相似故。」若依《纓絡》所說，虛空定即有五支。五支者，如經說：「一、想；二、護；三、正；四、觀；五、一心。」但上來四禪悉有支相貌可見，今此空定既無別證支離之法，此恐是據修空方便，義立為支，故經言：「方便道同，體用相似故。」餘經論悉不立支者，當是為自體無有別證支林成就之相，而於《纓絡》中說有支者，多是據方便及約義故說支。
en: Second, clarifying whether factors are present or absent: the various other sūtras and treatises, in clarifying the four formless concentrations, generally do not establish any factors for them at all; only the Yingluo Sūtra says: "Within the four concentrations of emptiness, five factors serve as the cause, and the sixth, the mind of silence, serves as the substance of concentration, the expedient path being the same, substance and function resembling one another." Following what the Yingluo Sūtra says, then, the concentration of empty space does indeed have five factors. These five factors, as the sūtra states, are: conception; guarding; correctness; contemplation; and one-pointedness of mind. But, whereas the four dhyānas already discussed above all had visibly distinct marks of their own factors, this concentration of emptiness has no such distinctly realized, branching dharma of its own — this is likely, then, spoken with reference to the expedient means for cultivating emptiness, factors established here only as a matter of convenient sense, hence the sūtra's own qualification: "the expedient path being the same, substance and function resembling one another." As for why the other sūtras and treatises generally do not establish factors here at all: this must be because, in its own substance, there is no distinctly realized, grove-of-factors-like mark of accomplishment present; and, as for why the Yingluo Sūtra speaks of factors being present, this, for the most part, is spoken with reference to expedient means and to sense alone.

zh: 約方便立支，其義云何？一、想者，修空定時，想身如簁如甑想。二、護者，即是捨支，捨於三種色相；又護者，名護持，遮三種色，不令破於空心。三、正者，不邪為義。今修空定為正，若念色相，是則為邪。四、觀者，觀達正念，破三種色，達於空理。若觀心住虛空，無有分散，名一心支。通明支者，謂支離為義，因此五法支離非一，故名為支。約修方便論支正應如此，佛意難知，既無的文，不可定判。或是證空定時，於空定中義立五支。何以故？經亦說言：「五支為因，第六默然心為定體。」今約修空立支隱顯，明因果體用，如似不便。若約證空定時，義立五支，亦復宛然，似如可見，深推自解，不煩多釋。
en: As for establishing factors with reference to expedient means, what is the sense of this? First, conception: while cultivating the concentration of emptiness, conceiving of the body as though it were a sieve or a steaming-basket. Second, guarding: this is precisely the factor of relinquishing, relinquishing the three kinds of mark of form; "guarding" also means maintaining and protecting, warding off the three kinds of form, not allowing them to break through the mind of emptiness. Third, correctness: this means being free of deviance — cultivating the concentration of emptiness here is what is correct; were one instead to dwell on the mark of form, this would be deviant. Fourth, contemplation: contemplating and penetrating right mindfulness, breaking through the three kinds of form, penetrating the principle of emptiness. Fifth, if the contemplating mind abides within empty space, free of any scattering, this is named the factor of one-pointedness of mind.

Explaining the general sense of "factor": this means the sense of branching apart — because these five dharmas branch apart from one another, not being a single unity, they are named "factors." Discussed with reference to the expedient means of cultivation, the sense of the factors should properly be exactly as given here; but the Buddha's own intent is difficult to know for certain, and, there being no definite text on the matter, this cannot be judged with full certainty. Alternatively, it may be that, at the very moment the concentration of emptiness is realized, five factors are established there as a matter of sense as well. Why is this? Because the sūtra likewise says: "The five factors serve as the cause, and the sixth, the mind of silence, serves as the substance of concentration." Here, establishing factors with reference to cultivating emptiness leaves cause and effect, substance and function, somewhat obscured and inconvenient to explain; but, if factors are instead established with reference to the moment emptiness is actually realized, in accordance with their own sense, this, too, seems entirely coherent and readily seen — examined closely, this may be resolved for oneself, and need not be explained further here.

zh: 第三、體用者，前五支為因，第六默然心為果，果後更起五支則為用，默然為體，例如前四禪不異。問曰：向言無證支，那得例上？答曰：還用方便支義支對，隱顯例作，亦當於義無失。第四、淺深者，初得虛空定，即離三種色，心與十方虛空相應，於後定既重發，復覺心識明淨，見空亦廣，定又增深。自覺初淺狹，今則漸廣深，如是乃至九品，類前可知。第五、進退者，得虛空定亦有四種人不同，所謂退分、住分、進分、達分，類如上四禪中說，今不廣明。第六、明功德者，亦有共、不共。共如上說。不共離過者，始於此空定中，方得離三種色過。善心不共者，得離色證空，更得增勝、信敬、慚愧等諸功德。
en: Third, as for substance and function: the first five factors serve as the cause, and the sixth, the mind of silence, serves as the effect; after this effect, the five factors arise once more, serving then as the function, with silence itself as the substance — exactly the same pattern as already given for the four dhyānas. Question: it was just said that there are no distinctly realized factors here at all — how, then, can this be treated the same as the dhyānas above? Answer: this simply uses the expedient-means sense of the factors as a corresponding parallel, obscured and revealed by the same pattern in turn — and this, too, should be without fault in its own sense.

Fourth, as for depth: upon first attaining the concentration of empty space, one leaves the three kinds of form behind, the mind corresponding with the ten directions' own empty space; afterward, as this concentration arises anew, one becomes aware once more of mind and consciousness growing bright and pure, the perception of emptiness itself growing ever broader, concentration itself growing ever deeper. Aware, at first, of shallowness and narrowness, and now of gradually growing breadth and depth — proceeding in this way all the way through nine grades, understood by the same pattern as already given.

Fifth, as for progress and regression: attaining the concentration of empty space likewise involves four differing kinds of practitioner — those prone to regression, those who abide, those who progress, and those who penetrate through — following the same pattern as already given within the four dhyānas above; this is not explained again here at length.

Sixth, clarifying merit: this too has both shared and distinct merit. The shared merit is as already described above. As for the distinct merit of freedom from fault: it is only beginning with this very concentration of emptiness that one is finally able to gain freedom from the fault of the three kinds of form. As for the distinct merit of a wholesome mind: having gained freedom from form and realized emptiness, one attains further excellent qualities still — faith, reverence, shame, remorse, and the other such merits.

The bird-escaping-its-cage simile marks a real threshold in the treatise's own imagery: every simile through the four dhyānas involved refinement within embodiment (a pool, a bell, a spring within rock); here, as in the bird leaving its cage already used in the discussion of sympathetic joy's merit, the image is of leaving the container itself behind. The uncertainty about whether the five "factors" genuinely apply to the formless concentrations at all — worked through at unusual length, with the treatise honestly admitting "the Buddha's own intent is difficult to know for certain" — is a rare moment of explicit interpretive humility, distinguishing what the source texts actually support from what this school's own systematic framework would prefer to find.

quiz.q: What simile describes the freedom of mind released from form upon realizing the space concentration?
options: a caged bird, the cage broken, flying freely
an inchworm at the branch tip
quiz.why: Free of form's bondage, mind is clear and unobstructed, like a bird flying from a broken cage. The inchworm and tethered bird describe falling back from the highest formless state.

quiz.q: According to the Yingluo Sūtra, what are the five factors of the space concentration?
options: inner clarity, joy, happiness, one-pointedness, concentration
quiz.why: The five are conception, guarding, correctness, contemplation, and one-pointedness, established largely with reference to the expedient means. Option B is the first dhyāna's factors.
